projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edward Langa was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: In 1941 I was living in Euclid, Ohio and I was a student at Shore High School, Euclid Shore, and I was in my senior year. I was 17 years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, were you 17 years old and still in school when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: That's correct. The Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7th in 1941. I was due to graduate in June of 1942, six months later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What are your memories of that day?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Well, quite a bit. First of all, I want to start out by saying that this is not going to be an Audie Murphy or John Wayne-type of story. This is just a story about an average high school kid who was willing and eager to do whatever was asked of him in the best -- to the best of his ability. So, getting back to the day of Pearl Harbor, in my senior year of high school I worked three nights a week at a drugstore on Nobel Road and Montecella Boulevard. To get there -- I worked Wednesdays, Saturdays and Sundays and I worked the 7:00 to 10:30 shift, 10:30 p.m. To get there I had to walk a mile to the bus, take a bus, get a transfer, transfer to another bus and then get to work. Seems like a lot of bother, but what the heck, I was making 40 cents an hour. So, anyhow, we were in the drugstore and my job at the drugstore -- it was an old fashioned drugstore that had a soda fountain, stools and some tables and they served up simple sandwiches and coffee and my job was to be the gofer for the woman who ran the soda bar and I also had the -- I sold cigarettes, cigars, tobacco, pipes, snuff, the newspapers and things like that. But any time I wasn't busy I was assigned to help this lady. And she was a very pretty middle aged lady of about 25 years old. I was 17 so anything above 20 is middle age and she was a very beautiful person from the inside out, as well. And we got along very well. But, on this particular day, there was no traffic in the drugstore and we just kept looking at each other wondering where everybody was. We had no TV in the -- of course, and no radio in the store and just once some guy popped in for a quick pack of cigarettes and he says, "Have you seen any Japs yet?" And after he left she and I just kind of looked at each other and shrugged our shoulders. You know, there's goofballs all over the place. Well, we closed up the store and she always gave me a ride to the half way point where I could only catch one bus and she had a small Plymouth coupe and she turned the radio on and that's when we found out about Pearl Harbor. So, instead of her driving me half way home, she drove me all the way home that night and dropped me off right in my driveway which was very nice of her. And -- I was surprised when I got home because the lights were still on and my mom and dad were still awake and they were huddled over the radio listening to this. And we just kind of looked at each other. Everybody was stunned. I didn't realize the full significance of the attack on Pearl Harbor, the devastation at that -- at that particular time. But -- so we went to bed and the next morning I got up early and everybody got to school early. My senior class was 104. Figure half of those were girls so that's 50 guys. We were all very closely knit. We knew one another. And all the guys got there early and we just gathered in a group and started to talk about this thing and, you know, we knew that college was down the drain for that -- for a while, anyhow. And so, we were contemplating, you know, what we were going to do and some guys wanted to jump ship and enlist right away. But fortunately, we had some wonderful teachers and they got into our discussion and they told us the best thing we could do would be to finish school, get our diploma and we would still get our chance. Two of the guys did jump. One went to the Royal Canadian Air Force but when they found out that he was under age and a runaway they shipped him back. And the other guy left for the Marines and he went to the South Pacific. But anyhow, not to get ahead of myself but out of that small group of 50 guys, three of them were killed in action. One was a pilot on a B17. My best buddy was a bombardier/navigator on a B29. He bombed Nagasaki before the A-bomb and one of them was a waist gunner on a B17. Now, the individual who jumped ship and tried to join the Royal Canadian Air Force, he came back and he got into our Air Force and he was a fighter pilot. And he got shot -- his plane got shot up and he was limping back to England and he bailed out over the English Channel but they rescued him right away and he went back to work, so to speak. One of the guys in my class had both legs blown off and came back and he was so determined that he actually danced at one of our class reunions. There were people who lost their lives in the classes ahead of me and the classes behind me. In the class behind me one of the guys that was on the hockey team with me just retired probably about eight months ago as a general. So, it was -- it was a good group -- group of guys. But, anyhow, so, I finished school and within a day or two after I got my diploma, I went down to downtown Cleveland and tried to enlist in the U. S. Navy. I wanted to be an aircraft mechanic on a -- on a -- what the heck --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Aircraft carrier?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Yes. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: The reason I did this is because I was hanging around open wheeled midget race cars from the time I was six years old and they tutored me and eventually I got to learn engines pretty good, racing engines, to the point where I could take them apart and be able to put them back together. But -- but anyhow, so they examined me and they said, "You have three teeth to be filled and one to be pulled. Go home and get it done and come back." And this staggered me. We're six months into a war and I can't get in because I needed three teeth to be filled. So I went home and I told my dad, I said, "Dad, I got to get this done right away." And he just looked at me and he says, "You know, just relax," he says, "they'll change their mind and come back to you." Well, it was -- by this time I had registered for the draft because I had turned 18. Wasn't long after that I got my greetings from the president and I was inducted into the service. And I like to say abducted because all of a sudden now I found I was in the U.S. Army, not the Navy. So, I took my first train ride of my life, went to Camp Kerr (ph) and they did the -- the ritual, the exams and the shots and all that good stuff and they outfitted you with clothes that were ill fitting. We looked like a ragtag army on a Halloween masquerade, you know. But then they interviewed me and I sat down in front of this officer and I didn't even know what rank he was but he asked me if I had any objections to being in the ground forces. And man, I jumped up out of my chair and shook his hands and I says, thank you, thank you, thank you, because in the back of my pointed little head -- I didn't know military terminology -- I thought he was going to put me in the ground crew of the Air Force. So, he looked at me very quizzically and he left the room and pretty soon another guy comes in and he was either a psychologist or psychiatrist. He wanted to see if I was playing with a full deck. Well, the next thing I know I'm on a train and I still think I'm in the Air Force. Two days later I arrive in Camp Waldress, Texas and lo and behold, I'm in an infantry replacement training center. And I thought to myself, how the hell are we ever going to win a war when they make stupid mistakes like this? So, anyhow, it turned out to be the best thing that ever happened to me because infantry basic at that time was 17 weeks and it was tough. But I was -- I was kind of a fitness nut. I never smoked, I never touched alcohol at all and because I played hockey and baseball and kept active all the time, I was in pretty good shape plus I was young. And so, it was -- it was great -- just a great training. At the end of --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'm just curious about when was it -- when did you go into the army?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Oh, this was early '43. Late '42, early '43.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it tough when you first went into basic training to be thrown in with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yes. I didn't -- didn't like that too much at all because you didn't know anybody and you were being trained as a replacement and when you finished training they sent you in little groups. Some would go to Indiantown Gap, Pennsylvania, others would go to San Luis Obispo, California and you were going to go fill in the holes that were left in some combat area. So that didn't appeal to me too much but I couldn't do much about it. So, anyhow, at the end of this basic, they held this battalion -- this was 1100 guys and they held 40 of us back and we didn't know why. They said because of academics. Okay. The next thing I knew, we were taking a test which was about like three hours long and it was -- I don't know whether it was an IQ test or just a general test or SAT test or something, you know, but out of the 40 they -- they took seven us and they sent us to specialized schools and -- engineering schools where we were taught college alg, physics, chemistry, English, history and geography and we went to school six days a week and we had mandatory study halls from 7:00 to 10:30 every night. So it was a -- we were being force fed. Well, got pulled out of there, sent back to Camp Robinson, Arkansas and now I was in the combat engineers. I was going to take combat engineer basic training. And I kept notes here. What is a combat engineer? Okay. "A combat engineer is a soldier who has been trained as an infantryman and then receives special training in a wide variety of engineering skills. He will operate in the frontal areas and in an emergency may be called upon to become a temporary infantryman." Now, I want to say right here I have the highest admiration in the world for infantrymen and by no stretch of the imagination were we -- were we equal. However, we'd make a pretty good help if they ever needed it. Okay. "Combat engineer is familiar with and can handle the M1 rifle, M1 carbine, the Browning automatic rifle, the M3 machine gun, Thompson submachine gun, .30 caliber light machine gun, .30 caliber water-cooled machine gun, .50 caliber machine gun, flame throw -- excuse me -- flame throwers and bazookas. All these weapons are part of each platoon as a combat engineer." However, in actuality we got very little chance to shoot back. Every time we got shot at we were in the middle of a project and we were depending on others to try to protect us. Okay? Now, "The engineering skills he masters covers a wide variety of demands. These include the building of stationary or fixed bridges, loading bridges, clearing enemy mine fields of land mines, anti personnel mines and deactivating booby traps. In a defensive posture he can lay a protective mine field as requested. He is also expert at demolitions including TNT, dynamite, nitrostarch, ammonium nitrate and the plastic explosive, C4. He is qualified and licensed to drive jeeps, three-quarter ton, ton and a half, two and a half ton and four ton trucks. He can, in an emergency, operate a D8 bulldozer." But not very well. He can move it frontwards or backwards. "Combat engineers are very mobile and can be sent to any area where their expertise is needed. As previously stated, these areas are in the combat areas. Combat engineers are not -- not to be confused with heavy equipment engineers who build more permanent structures such as railroad bridges, et cetera. "The heavy equipment engineers operate in safe, stabilized areas where their cranes and other specialized equipment can be used to full advantage." So -- okay. So now I've had -- I've gone through the combat engineering basic which I sailed through because I've had the previous infantry basic and these guns and everything were second nature to me. And so, the next thing I know, they put me in -- they were starting a new combat engineering battalion in Camp Robinson, the 259th, and I was a corporal already, okay. So, now, my job was to help train these new guys. And pretty soon I worked my way up and before I was 19 and a half years old, I was a platoon sergeant. Okay? So, the 259th then moved on. And again, I was held back plus some other cadre and we were sent to Texas to form another combat engineering battalion and company -- in my case, company. Now, for once the army did something right because the guys they were sending us were the guys from upper Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin. They were all hunters, good shots, and they -- they were not the flat bellied prototype picture soldier that you see on a poster, you know, poster boy. These guys were more burly, strong, they worked in construction and they were -- they were just a God send. Not all of them, but the majority that I got were this type people. The rest of them were fillers, some from other outfits, some from the MPs that were declared surplus but they were pretty big, as well. And so they were all strong. And I liked this outfit and -- and I requested that -- I wanted to stay -- no more of this jumping around. I wanted to stay with this group. Well, we finished up our training and this training included the Bailey bridge, you know, which is a prefab erector-type bridge and the bridges we built here in the States were across a ravine or small river but where you could build a whole bridge on one side and roll it across on rollers, put the rollers on the other side and jack up the bridge, take the rollers out and make your ramps and you had a go. So, that was good. And we also built timber bridges and everything. And so, next thing you know, we're on our way to New York. And thank God, because I didn't want to go to the Pacific. And I guess we went to Camp Shanks which was a port of embarkation. But we got liberty in -- in New York City, and this was one of my failings because when I got to New York City, I did the usual tourist thing. I went to Rockefeller Center and I went to a few night clubs and what I should have done was gone to some store and get a map of Europe. Now, that sounds crazy but I just assumed that when we got over there we were going to get maps and everything would be provided. Well, that was wrong and that was -- I learned very quickly, never assume anything. If you want something done, you better do it yourself or get it yourself and if by any chance they -- they should supply you with something, it's redundant, so what. So you have got two. So anyhow, so we went back to Camp Shanks after this liberty and waited around. We had a couple of just dry runs where you form the company and take them to the train that was going to take you to the docks and then they'd fly back out and tell you sit on your bunks for a while. And this happened two or three times. It was very aggravating. Finally, it really happened. And by this time it was getting kind of dusk. We got on the train, got on -- took us to the docks, we got on the boat and that was kind of a shocker because troop ships, geez, they had these pipe racks about four or five high, narrow aisles, maybe 30 inches and you had all your equipment, your rifle, and you were supposed to just get in there, throw them on your bunk, and climb up there and stay there so the other people could pass, you know. And this is where I found out that -- this gets to be claustrophobic and I found out, thank God, I'm not a submariner. But -- but you also realize, too, that with -- with crowds like that, in an emergency, you'd never reach the top deck. Your -- your fate was in the hands of God. So, one of the things I wanted to see desperately was the Statue of Liberty. But we were so exhausted and -- and -- from all this rigamarole, fell asleep and got up and ran up on deck. All I saw was water. We were gone. And for 14 more days, all we saw was water. We were traveling in a convoy and that was quite an experience. You would see ships and you wouldn't see them, the waves would come up and you would swear the little destroyer went underneath and would never come up again and somehow he did, you know, or it did, she did, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you make that crossing?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you make that crossing?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: November of '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '44. Okay.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. I think. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything happen on that crossing, any sub scares or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: No. Just rough weather. And I think it was November, maybe it was earlier. Anyhow, we got to South Hampton, England and from there they put us on a train and all the blackout curtains were drawn and we were going somewhere and we ended up in a little place called Adelstrop which was near Stonewall which was near Morton on the Marsh. But -- actually, it was -- closest big city was Cheltenham and Oxford and they were about 30 miles away. And we stayed in quonset huts and we did some more training and then by this time, they had come out with a new wrinkle called a floating Bailey bridge where they kept this same bridge that we were building but they built it on pontons (sic). Now, the word is p-o-n-t-o-o-n-s, pontoons, but engineers call them pontons. Okay. So, these pontoons are made of three plywood sections, boxes, if you wish, a center section and an end section. Each section is 20 feet long and each section weighs 2,000 pounds. The front and the trailing edge have a little ramp for the water, you know, little pointed nose. But -- so, our job was to learn how to build these bridges and they had three sites set up and we had to build a bridge across the Thames river and take it down and stack it and we were through. And we had -- at first it was a real dog, you know. We were unfamiliar with this and -- but the river was only 400 feet. And eventually we got little bit better and we moved to another site and we did this and we did this and we did this and pretty soon we were getting our bridge up and done like 1:00 o'clock in the afternoon. Now, I have to tell you a little bit about this bridge. It's -- again, it's a prefab bridge like an erector set. But everything is hand carried. For every ten foot of bridge there are four panels, you know, structural panels. These panels are five foot high by 10 feet long, they weigh 600 pounds. They were carried by guys. You put three carrying bars through there and six guys grab on there and they lift it and carry it to the bridge and set it in place, go back, get another one. Anyhow, it -- it worked out. But -- so, we knew there was going to be kind of a bridge in our future someplace. So, eventually we left from Waymouth, England and we crossed the Channel in an LST. All our trucks and everything were on this LST, and that was -- it was a very rough crossing. I remember that. That Channel gets rough. But, we -- they beached at Le Havre and opened up the gates, the front doors, and we drove off, you know, and we went to a place called Camp Lucky Strike, I think it was, where it's just a marshalling area and we stayed the night and kind of got organized and we were issued ammunition then for our first fire fight. Nobody was allowed to carry ammunition on any ship. So we got all our ammo and loaded our trucks and trailers with ammo and we started into France and we did anything that was asked of us. Now, we were actually in the Third Army which was Patton's army, but we were corps troops. We weren't assigned to any particular division. Anyplace they needed a job done, you know, we were like Mr. Roto-Rooter, hey. So, that's where we went. And we did some mine field clearing and some booby traps and things of that but we kept going on in, you know, nothing spectacular. And then we stopped and the company commander called -- I was platoon sergeant, as I said. He called the three platoon sergeants from A Company and the three platoon lieutenants and we went up, got up, snuck up and he says this is our job and we saw the Rhine river. He says, we're going to have to put a bridge across there that will support a tank column. And I looked at that river and I said holy sh -- smokes. You could hardly see from one side of the bank to the other. And -- and you think back to the dinky little 400 footer that we built and this river is running eight to 10 miles an hour, we could see stuff floating through and it was gone. And he says, "A-Company is going to be the head honcho on this and we're going to assign all the work tasks. We're all going to do all the ramrodder -- ramrodding. We had the whole battalion to draw from as far as labor. And so, the next day or two, we were -- that is, the six of us, seven of us with the company commander -- busier than hell because you don't carry that kind of equipment with you. You have to arrange for it and you have to figure out where the bridge -- actual bridge is going to be, where your work sites are going to be and the work sites are downstream. If you build a small 10 foot floating section and you attach a motor to it or you pull it and you bring it up into the place, pin it, you know. So, the -- just the logistics. These pontoons, like I said, are -- each section is 20 feet long and weigh -- four feet wide, five feet wide, maybe, and weighs a ton. And they had to be transported to these sites. So, maybe Red Ball was involved in this, I don't know, but they had semis come in with flatbeds and these things were stacked up and that was the only mechanical-type tool we had. They had some kind of a crane that would take these off the semis and set them on the bank and from then on we had to slide them to the water. So, we got started and when I say we -- we were drawing from the whole battalion. Let me say this. A company of combat engineers is 167 people, 167 men. Of that 167, oh, maybe 140 are line people. The rest are support. You have the cook and the bakers and the captain, driver and the supply sergeant, company clerk, the assistant supply sergeant. And so, that -- that whole ratio was -- was prevalent through the whole battalion. There are three companies in a battalion plus headquarters and supply company in a battalion. And so we, you know, set up these work parties and went at it. Now, when I said we never had a chance to shoot back, on the opposite side of the river was -- this was -- was -- this was in the rural area and on the open side of the area was a rural pocket. The Germans were surrounded. We had a few crazies. Most of them would -- would give up, I guess, if they -- you know, if they had a chance but they were surrounded and they were kind of ignoring us and occasionally we would take some kind of fire but we had tanks that were dug in around us and we had anti aircraft. Now, I thought the German Air Force was all kaput by this time and I guess really, it was, but we were supposed to be protected so, like I said, we never had a chance to shoot back. Just go ahead and do your work. Occasionally something would come in and everybody would hit the deck and -- but then you get up and start working again. So, as we -- this bridge, I guess -- I messed up here. This bridge was between Langhausen and Duisberg, Germany is on the east bank, is the largest inland port in Germany. They had ocean going vessels come in there. So, it was -- it was a big industrialized area. And as we built this bridge we said we need to get away from the -- the bank and get out into the current. Of course, the current is going to take your bridge and move it down -- downstream. So, we had to have anchors and we used anything we could get our hands on for an anchor. We had a truck that had an oxygen acetylene torch on it and small jib hoist and he was going up and down the river. Anything he saw that had a suitable anchor he'd burn it off and bring it to us. And so we'd bring a floating section into place and we'd take one of these anchors that -- with a long cable, take it about a couple hundred feet, maybe 250 feet upstream, drop it and then use this cable and we had a transit set up and signals and the guys would be -- had to come along and they would be hoisting this thing up until where it was and then cinch it and that's how we kept our bridge from having any kind of a bow. If anything, we wanted just a little bit of a hog which was kind of an arch which would help support it against the current, you know. So we built the bridge and it would accommodate 25 Sherman tanks at one time, rolling tanks, and it was quite scary when they -- when they first went over. You know, this was -- I felt this was my bridge and if that thing failed and it was -- one of those tank went down, I think I would have had to commit suicide, you know. But it turned out well. It was a single lane bridge and just to give you a little bit of an idea of the weight we handled, I just did a quick calculation and a very conservative, very, very conservative estimate is that we manhandled 692,000 pounds of steel. That's 346 tons of everything by hand. Plus this doesn't include the pontoons which were -- like I say, to make one pontoon 60 foot long you've got three tons. So that's the type of thing we did. And after the bridge was built -- it was a one-way bridge. So we had to direct traffic and we stayed there for three or four days making sure that everything was all right and we had a crew on the bridge 24 hours a day, maintenance crew, just going from one end to the other checking everything and then on each end of the bridge we had a telephone radio operator. And he -- they had to direct traffic. You know, some would be going east and some would be coming back maybe in an ambulance or maybe something. And we had to keep track of all of the traffic and what went over in which direction and also the level of the river. You know, the snow cap was starting to melt on the mountains and the river was going to rise. And as this river would rise, there's a landing bay that goes from the water to the bank and this would be -- you know, as the river would rise, the end of the bridge at the very bank would be moving backwards. So this whole thing was built -- the bridge had a sliding base plate and it would accommodate a three foot rise and fall in the river bank -- in the river level. And so, it -- it -- you know, I don't know how the hell we did it. I really don't. If I had to do it today, I'd say it was impossible. And I -- I look back at some of these things and it can't be done, it just can't be done. But we did it. So, another interesting thing here is that I volunteered for the 11:00 to 7:00 shift, 11:00 at night to 7:00 in the morning, and we also had guys stationed in every other pontoon and they had a case of ammunition and an M1 rifle and anything that came floating down the river they were to shoot at it and -- because we were worried about the Germans sending down floating mines and taking out the bridge. And then further upstream, probably a quarter of a mile, there was a great big, oh, depression, if you wish, which made natural cover. We had a boat with an outboard motor and it was loaded with explosives and we had a crew there 24 hours a day and anything that came down large, they were supposed to go out there, slap a charge on it and sink it. And that's how much we were worried about -- about this bridge being destroyed. And so, during this course of the evening shift we had to take a report back to group headquarters which -- or Corps headquarters, I'm sorry -- which was about eight or 10 miles behind us which doesn't sound like a lot but on secondary roads and you're not sure where you're going and it becomes kind of chancy at night, too. We had -- the jeeps had these wire cutters on the bumpers because the Germans were famous for putting the wire across at about neck height and you go flying through with the jeep and you leave your head behind. So, the guys I sent the first night, they said they got shot at on this trip so I said well, I'll go from here on in and I had my jeep driver and we take this back and every once in a while I swear we got shot at but we traveled -- and we varied our times and we traveled without lights. But this one night coming back -- this is the humorous part of it -- we had to cross the railroad track and there was no rail track and this one night we were coming back to the bridge and all of a sudden we see this train across the road and it was stopped and there were people milling around and it was past -- you know, this was late at night and we hit the brakes and we dove into the ditch, you know, into the ditch on the side of the road. We didn't know what was coming off. And my jeep driver turned to me and said, "Sarge," he says, "I forgot my damn machine gun. It's in the jeep." Well, on the dashboard of the jeep he had a mount for a Thompson sub and that's where it was. So he crawl -- he crawled back up there and got it and we worked our way up to where these people were and we saw a GI helmet and we knew that okay, these weren't any bad guys. And it turned out that these were slave workers who had been displaced and they were being taken back and the train had stopped for some unknown reason, I guess, and these guys were out relieving themselves, you know. You know, we would have shot the whole troop. But that was it. Then we -- somebody else came in -- come up and took over this maintenance job on the bridge and we moved on. And I got another job to build a -- this was my platoon -- to build a Class 70 bridge in a small village that was literally divided by a stream and the bridge was blown plus all the buildings around it were blown and they wanted to put a bridge across that would -- a Class 70 bridge that would support a semi and a flatbed and a Sherman tank and they were going to use this road to bring back disabled Sherman tanks and recover and this was a timber bridge, a wooden bridge. So, it was a cushy job. It was a cushy job because it was safe. There didn't seem to be anybody around and, gee, you couldn't ask for anything better. And I milked that and, you know, about three or four days longer than I should have because my guys were tired and the company commander knew what I was doing. But he was a great guy. I'd follow him right to hell. He didn't say anything and -- so, that ended well. And we built a bridge and all of a sudden there were some German civilians popped up and they said, you know, "Could we put an asphalt deck -- you know, layer on that wood?" And I says, "It's not going to work but be my guest, I don't care, I'm gone." And I don't know whether they ever did or not but it was a nice bridge. I'm sure it would have held the 70 tons that they asked. So, we did a few more odds and ends like, you know, check for mines, pick up some mines, clear a couple of booby traps. Then one other thing I have to tell you is the reason I didn't -- I said I failed, I didn't get a map of Europe, we never knew where the hell we were. So, when they say, "Sergeant Langa, take your platoon and go here and there's a job waiting for you," they'd give you a little strip of paper about an inch wide and just shows you a road and a couple of little towns in between. Well, you know, you start to go and -- and the next thing you know, the road is blocked because of the buildings had been bombed out and the road is just full of rubble and you have to go around. Well, you don't know which way to turn, left or right. You don't know where the good guys are or the bad guys are. And, you know, you sure as heck don't want to lead your group into an ambush. So, you know, it got so that whenever -- whenever possible I would go and scope the job out before I brought any people up. In the first place, you didn't want to bring up a whole platoon if the squad could handle it. I learned quickly, and it was something that stuck with me through my whole life, you never send three men on a job -- on a two-man job because two of them are going to stand around bullshit -- bull talking -- excuse me -- talking, while one guy is working and it's going to take twice as long. So, that's what I did whenever I could. And this one time we got a job and we're supposed to go into Dusseldorf and so the platoon lieutenant and I were going to scope it out and, you know, bring back the necessary people. Well, Dusseldorf was already captured and the area we were in was kind of like a ghost town. Didn't see anybody, it was just a ghost town. And all of a sudden we looked and way off in the distance here's this guy and he's walking and turned the corner out of our view and he had one of these gray -- gray coats on, long coats, one of the Hitler swoopy-type hats on and we looked at each other and we said that's got to be SS. This guy is, you know, infiltrating the lines. So, we -- we -- we separate and we made up our plan and we tracked him and all of a sudden we jumped out at this guy, both of us, and I want to tell you, he went about six feet straight up in the air. Well, it wasn't SS at all. It was some old guy probably about 70, 80 years old and the hat -- he had on a little brass plate on the front and a picture of a trolley car strausbaun (ph), you know, he was a streetcar conductor trying to conduct. The lieutenant looked at me and I looked at him and he says, "Sarge," he says, "if you ever tell anybody about this, I'll kill you." I says, "Don't worry." So, Lieutenant, if you're still around and you hear this, I'm not going to tell you where I live. Then the war ended on May 8th of '45, and things were changed all -- you know, pretty radically. Now all of a sudden we could no longer wear our fatigues, our grungy old fatigue. We had to be in Class A which was wool ODs and sometime we had to wear ties. And -- but we were one of the first outfits that were pulled back out and we kind of retraced our routes and had a chance to go back over the same bridge we built which was kind of neat. And then we went to pull back into southern France into a place called Arles, Arles Station area, A-r-l-e-s, maybe it's Arles, I can't -- I don't know how the French pronounce it. It's near Marseilles, you know, north of Marseilles. And we were told that -- you know, we were a good outfit. That's not -- not bragging. We were a good outfit. And we were told we were going to figure in the invasion of Japan. And that gets a little scary because no matter how good you are you've got to be lucky.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. So, you were told you would be involved in the invasion of Japan; right?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: That's correct. Now, combat engineers have a two and a half ton truck for every squad and as a platoon there are three two and a half ton GMC's plus a jeep, plus a trailer plus a weapons carrier and that's one platoon. Now, there's three platoons in a company and there's three companies in a battalion and then you have headquarters area and supply -- you know, there are vehicles plus each company has a D8 bulldozer with a -- with a flatbed and a four ton Diamond T Prime Mover. All this equipment was brought in and had to be brought back into first-class shape and be prepared for a salt water travel. And, you know, piece by piece by piece, everything was refurbished, stuff that could be was cosmoline wrapped in waterproof paper and put in crates. And also, at the same time they brought guys from the South Pacific that had -- veterans of the Japanese war and they were teaching us about Japanese weaponry and Japanese mines and booby traps and -- because that was going to be our job. So, it -- it took some time. Let's see, we got pulled out of Germany in May and in August we had sent our trucks and everything on a freighter which was going to go to Manila and that's where we were going to meet them, in the Philippines, Manila, and we were being subjected to further training. Well, pretty soon we got a troop ship, the "GENERAL BRECKENRIDGE" I think the name of it was, that pulled into Marseilles and we went down there and loaded on. Just about that time they dropped the first A-bomb on Hiroshima and I don't think we really knew it until we were on board ship. So, we were going to -- we left Marseilles and we were sailing on the Mediterranean and it was one of the most pleasant cruises I was ever on. The water was so blue, the sun was nice and warm and we were up on deck and we were watching the dolphins follow the ship and when we got into the Straits of Gibraltar you could see Europe on one side and Africa on the other. And then we headed out into a southwesterly direction, I guess for the Panama Canal, but all of a sudden they told us the second bomb was dropped on Nagasaki and the Japanese surrendered and they turned the boat and brought us into New York Harbor which yea. But that -- that return trip was nine days as compared to 14 going over. And we traveled that trip home alone, not in convoy. And when we got to New York Harbor, the fire boats came out to meet us and the sprays were going and there was the Statue of Liberty then. It never looked so good. Anyhow, we went along the coastline into -- into New Jersey and we docked in New Jersey and one of the things that astounded us all was that it was a highway that -- that you could see from the ship and it paralleled the coastline and these cars were going so darn fast. We thought what the hell's happened since we've been gone. These people have gone crazy. You know, they must have been traveling 50 or 60 miles an hour but it seemed like they were on a -- on a race car -- race course. So we pulled into Camp Kilner and the first thing they did was took us in the mess hall and we ate steak and ice cream and milk until you couldn't eat anymore, until they rolled you out of there. It was just great. It was surprising, even a guy like me, I think I had two steaks but some of the bigger guys could really put it away. And I never milk -- missed milk that much but those guys we're drinking it by the gallon. So, then, they -- next day or so -- we stayed the next day or so. They took us into a great big, I guess it was a field house where they had different stations and you'd go to one station and it would be -- a guy would take your measurements, give you a shirt that fit you and you would go to the next one and get a pair of trousers that fit you and if they didn't fit the guy would cuff them right there, they had tailors. And then you got a blouse and they -- they sewed on your correct insignias and they gave you a cap, military cap, and put your -- the ribbons that you earned on your chest and they -- then they sent you home for 30 or 45 days. But when you went home, you were supposed to look like a soldier. And then after the R and R at home, I went back to Camp Haus, Texas and -- I believe it was Camp Haus, either Camp Haus or Camp Bowie, they all run together, and we had to deactivate the outfit. And -- well, excuse me. Way back when I was still in Germany and -- and we lost our 1st sergeant. He had the misfortune with a jeep and a mine and I was platoon sergeant and all of a sudden I became 1st sergeant. So, now instead -- at that point, instead of a platoon I had 167 guys. I was 1st sergeant. So when I came back down at Camp Haus, I had to -- we had to deactivate the outfit. What remaining equipment, the rifles had to be turned in, every -- every piece of military equipment had to be turned in. Stupid me, I turned in my watch that was issued to me and I loved that thing because at one time there in the Rhine river, we got capsized because we tried to avoid some fire and I was in the river with the company commander. He and I were in the same boat and the water was so cold and the river, like I said, was running eight, 10 miles an hour and we were being swept downstream. Now, it doesn't take long for your combat boots to fill up with water and they were like cement shoes. But I got rid of my helmet, I got rid of my carbine. I saw it float for about six feet on top of the water and disappear. I got rid of my cartridge belt and canteen and I was trying to stay afloat and another boat came up and threw a line and the company commander got it, naturally, and they were pulling him in. And well, then, a very good friend of mine threw me a line that was just a skinny thing and I -- I grabbed it in one hand and somehow I wound it around my wrist because I was exhausted already. And every time they'd pull I could see the cord get a little thinner. They'd pull and -- and, you know, regroup and pull and regroup and so by the time I got to the side of the boat, I was helpless. They just had to pull me in and lay me down at the bottom and that doggone watch never stopped running. That just amazed me. This was back before water-tight watches, you know. It was a Waltham, I guess. But anyhow, when I was in the river, I said geez, I hope I get hit by a bullet. My mother would be so disappointed to find out I had came all the way over here to drown, you know. So that was -- that was weird. But then my wife and I got married in Brownwood, Texas and we honeymooned in San Antone, came back and finished up to where the whole outfit was disbursed to separation centers and then -- then I went. And my separation center was Camp Atterbury, Indiana. I think that was probably the most disappointing thing in my whole army career was that you went there and just lollygagged around and then pretty soon you were told to be in front of the mess hall at a certain time, like 6:00 o'clock. You were there and they had this little phonograph with a scratchy record, the guy would pop a needle down and it would play some kind of a march and you went to the mess hall. Then here was a 2nd lieutenant and just looked at him and you knew he couldn't have been in the army any longer than three months, four months, and he says, "Oh, I'm proud of you guys and here's your separation packets and from now on you're all civilians," and that was it. Didn't even shake hands with anybody. You know, it was -- it was kind of disappointing. It was a let down. So, they furnished transportation into Indianapolis and from then on you were on your own and I came home. But basically that's -- that's what happened to me. Like I said, no Audie Murphy stuff but just an average kid just doing an average job. And the thing is, that you see so many guys that do -- they're not buried yet, you know, when you're over there on both sides. And I don't know. It's -- it's -- those are the -- those are the real guys, the real heroes, you know. When we landed at Le Havre, we came across the Channel and landed at Le Havre, prior to that we were in England and reading the "Stars and Stripes" and they would -- had some pretty good glowing accounts of how we were, you know, winning the war and we hit the beach and -- and we started -- you know, the fighting had already gone. But you look around at the wreckage. There are tanks and airplanes and trucks and everything that was U. S. equipment was all shot to hell and the first thing you say is, who the heck is kidding who? You know, who's winning this war? But there's only one other thing that I can think of that was kind of a unique experience. We were in Germany and we didn't even know there was such a thing as a jet aircraft and all of a sudden, just (swish), we got buzzed by this German jet. He never fired a shot. I don't know why. Maybe he didn't have ammo, maybe -- we got buzzed and he was gone before we even knew he was coming. And we looked at each other and we says, you know, that thing didn't have any propellers. And, of course, then the rumors get started, well, that's just one of Hitler's secret weapons. And we thought, Oh, boy, we're going to get pushed back again, you know, we thought, gee whiz. But that was our first experience with a jet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned losing that 1st sergeant. Did you lose any other close buddies?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: No. No. I brought all my guys home. Some with a few punctures but they all come home. The other companies, I don't know how they fared. I know the outfit that -- from Camp Robinson, they went to the Pacific. They lost quite a few.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about clearing the mine field, could you describe how that's done?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Yeah. There's only -- the -- the mine -- the -- that was a war in itself, okay? We came out with a metallic mine detector and the Germans came out with non metallic mines. So we came out with a non metallic mine detector and the Germans would come out with plastic mines. And then they would just bury things that would give a signal and it might be just a big rock. So, the safest way was just to get down and probe with -- on your hands and knees and probe with a bayonet and the standard way we had of doing this was one guy would get a long white tape attached to his belt and he'd get on his hands and knees and start probing and after he got up, you know, 20 or 30 yards then two other guys would do the same thing on his flanks. And that would clear a path for a vehicle or anything else. Now, if this guy accidentally got blown up, the next guy would just follow the tape up there and attach it to his belt and keep on going. But, we had -- oh, we had a tank, for instance, that was designed with two booms out in front and a -- and a drum and to the drum was attached chains and this drum would rotate and these chains would beat on the ground and when it would come across a mine it would explode. But the Germans figured out the distance from the drum to the center of the bottom of the tank and they would lay a charge but the firing device would be forward of that charge so the tank would hit this charge and nothing would happen and it would roll on and hit the firing device and now all of a sudden this charge that was directly underneath the tank would blow and blow out the bottom of that tank. There was also another method where we had like corrugated pipe that was filled with explosives and it had a great big flexible -- there was a great big flexible ball. Now, the first few sections of this pipe were filled with sand and a tank would push it and then back up and they would put another section in, push it and back up and this thing would go on. It would be a snake, you know, for -- for whatever left you needed. And then after this whole thing was in place, there was a firing device out there on one of these sections and a tank would take a machine gun and hit the firing device and this whole thing would just blow a trench, a great big long trench, and you would just surge through the trench. But the -- when you lay a mine field, you almost -- always are required to make a map in case you have to pick up your own mines and we could never find any of the German maps. A lot of times one small area through a village would be cleared and you'd just get the civilian population and you kind of scared them a little bit and say, where are these mines and they'd show you because they watched them being put in place and they could go through these fields pretty safely. The only thing they had to worry about were these anti personnel mines and booby traps. And -- and originally the Germans came out with this teller mine which was kind of like a soup plate with a handle on the end because that way a guy could carry four of them, two in each hand, and on the top was a mushroom-type screw -- screw cap and that cap would come off and there would be a hole in this explosive and they would lay this firing device down there, screw this cap back on and this firing device had a plunger and when the weight came down and it pushed the plunger down and the thing would explode. Well, that was pretty good for us because you could take these mines, unscrew the tops, take out the firing device and throw it away and, you know, you were home free. Well, then, the Germans came out with a modified firing device that had a plunger on each end, okay? So now they screwed this mushroom cap on there and now if a pressure came down on that the mine would explode or if you unscrew that cap, the bottom one would trigger the mine and it would -- would blow you all to hell. So, Eisenhower come out with a dictate that nobody should try to deactivate a teller mine after that. So anyhow, then they had these nice carrying handles on and you could always attach a rope to it, you know, dig around this mine, attach a rope to it and -- and carry it off to the side and blow it at your convenience. But -- or just -- just carry it away. But then the Germans came out with another thing that they set underneath this teller mine and it was a firing device. Now, you -- you could get a signal and dig down and know that it's a teller mine and you could dig down a little bit further and you know there's a firing device underneath it and if you wanted to be really stupid you could pick both of them up together but nobody in the world was going to be around you when you tried to separate the two. So, in cases like that we'd put a rope on, give them a jerk and they'd explode. But then they would lay these things on the approach to a bridge or someplace where if you explode it you're going to impair traffic. And in that case the only thing you can do is build a ramp over them. It was -- it was a constant battle, this mine technology, mine and booby trap technology. All kinds of --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were some of the booby traps that you would encounter?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Well, a lot of trip wires, a lot of trip wires and some were the kind that were loose where you'd give them a push or a jerk or catch them with your foot and they would explode. Others were taut. If you cut them with a wire cutter they would explode. So you had to determine which was which. And the Germans also had a little shoe mine which was a little wooden mine and they found out in the war that it's no good to kill an enemy because he's dead. You just leave them there until somebody could take care of them. But, if you blow off his leg, now he's got to have immediate attention and then you tie up a corpsman and stretcher bearers, an ambulance and doctors and everything. So, the shoe mines were designed just to go after them and they worked. They also had bouncing betties that would shoot up in the air and then explode and scatter shrapnel down. And they even had stock mines which were just a concrete cast cylinder but in the cylinder was nails, anything, embedded in the concrete. And it had a hole, a core, and they just set these on a piece of broomstick with a -- with a trip wire and that's -- that was one type especially around the beaches. You saw that around the beaches. Yeah. That was a whole war in itself. You had to stay right with it. So anyhow, my salvation was -- I still say was the infantry basic I had and I had the opportunity to go through several different basic training periods so I felt I was, you know, qualified.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of mail call?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Mail call? Yeah. I can't speak for any other area but the areas that we were in, all our mail was censored. You had to write on one side of a sheet of paper, you couldn't write on both sides. All your mail was read and things were razored out. Any reference to where you were, what you did, outfit numbers, town -- town names was razored out. So, you -- it got so you wrote the stock letter, gee, don't worry about me, I'm doing fine, I'm being fed, I'm warm, everything like that. That was your -- your standard letter. As far as photographs, practically no one had cameras and those that did, I don't know how they got the pictures developed and if any pictures were sent back home, they all had to be stamped on the back censor approved. You know, any -- any picture of a tank, for instance, with an outfit designation on was -- was prohibited. Then when the people wrote to us, they had no idea where we were. I worked out a little code ahead of time. My folks knew I was in Germany just by this code. But, mail was sent to an APO, New York, army post office in New York, and from there on, I don't know how it reached us but it did, eventually. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your code, did you have some kind of a certain --

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Yeah. You know, I told them that the first letter of every sentence in the first paragraph was -- was like Germany. I started out with gee whiz, it's good to get your last letter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's good. Did they send you any memorable packages or anything?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Gosh, once we got -- my mom sent me canned chicken and that was good. Really good -- Some of the guys were getting bread but in this -- sometimes in this loaf of bread would be hollowed out and there would be a bottle of booze or something, you know. I -- will say this. We had our own cooks and bakers that traveled with us and they had field kitchens. Had a mess sergeant, his name was Goslin. We used to call him Goose, Goose Goslin. There was a baseball player by that name. Most conscientious guy, best guy -- best guy I ever encountered in all my life. He did his best -- to -- to keep us fed. And -- and ironically, when he came back, he took sick and they found out he had tuberculosis. And he was a mess sergeant -- yeah. And he died. He was put in a sanitarium and he died shortly after. Again, this is kind of discombobulated but one of the guys I graduated with, nice kid, he -- and all man. I mean, he was a waist gunner on a B17 and we both got R and R at home after war's end at the same time and I met him and his fingers were all brown from nicotine. He just was a chain smoker and he could hardly light the cigarette, his hands would tremble and, you know, that didn't make him any less brave. He just saw too much. So, anyhow, turned out -- nice guy, everybody liked him. He got his good job, was a salesman and about three or four weeks in civilian life he got killed by a drunk driver. One guy in the class below us, handsome kid, we all thought he was going -- true Hollywood material. He joined the Marines and went to the South Pacific and took a lot of shrapnel through his face and he come back looking like Quasimodo.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life when you came back?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Well, when we -- at the separation center, they told us, you know, if you've got any kind of an ailment, just let us know and we'll keep you for a couple, three weeks and we'll see that it's taken care of. So naturally, everybody was in the best of health. We were all anxious to get back into civilian life. You know, I was married and we were pregnant and I had written to a place where I used to work summers -- in the summers in high school, I used to work full time at a machine shop with my dad. We made forging machines and presses. And so, I had taken mechanical drawing in school and I had a pretty natural talent in that area. And so I wrote the president of the company while I was still in the service and he wrote back to me and he says, "Don't worry, you've got a job here from day one as soon as you get back." Well, he was -- he kept his word and I got a job in the engineering department and they were going to make a draftsman out of me. And the manager of engineering was a Case grad and he didn't take too kindly to being told that he had to sign me on into his group. So, they come up with a plan that was going to take 6,000 hours to become a draftsman. And it was good except no matter what I did, I was still Jasper's boy and here I just came back from oversees, had 167 guys and I couldn't do anything up there without somebody watching over my shoulder to make sure that I wasn't going to make a little teeny mistake, you know. It -- it -- it rankled me a little bit. But the only thing to do was that I -- I came back and -- and had one day of vacation and went to work the next day. I had no clothes. My kid brother used them all with my blessing and I didn't have any money to buy any. So I tore off all the chevrons and the insignias and I wore my uniform to work. Didn't have an overcoat for a couple of months until they -- they always held back two weeks pay, anyhow -- until I got my first pay check. But those -- those were difficult times. As a 1st sergeant I was making with my longevity, seniority, et cetera, 139 a month. And when this fellow interviewed me, he said we're going to start you out at one and a quarter and I thought that was a dollar and a quarter an hour and I -- the wheels turned. That's 160, 170 dollars a month. I came home and we celebrated like crazy, you know. My first paycheck I found out it was a hundred and a quarter a month. I took a cut in pay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experience does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Gosh, there's lots of them. But is there -- all I can say is I was glad -- glad that I did it. I was proud that I did it. Yeah. It's -- it -- excuse me -- I have -- I just got discombobulated from my thoughts. Anyhow, in reality, army life, outside of combat, isn't all that bad. It's kind of a simple life. There's three actions. If it moves, salute it; if it doesn't move, pick it up; if you can't pick it up, paint it. And there are three responses, yes, sir, no, sir, no excuse, sir. The other thing is black and white. So it was not that bad. You're always out -- they keep you in good shape and I was glad for the experience and I really feel sorry as hell for the guys that really had it tough and especially for the ones that didn't make it back. That's why I'm going to go to the World War II dedication here in May, the memorial. I just feel I owe it to the guys that didn't make it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think that covers it.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: That's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: There is one thing, it's stranger than fiction. It is stranger than fiction. When I got down to -- to Camp Bowie and we were starting this new outfit, the 1st sergeant and I went to the field house after -- after chow in the evening. Since we were walking around and all these fillers were in there and they were -- some of them were playing basketball but there was this fight going on where this great big guy had suckered this skinny guy into a fight. And he was knocking hell out of this skinny guy and every time this guy would get knocked out and he'd get up again and he would have fought until he died. So we broke up the fight and I told the 1st sergeant, "I want that man." And sure enough, I got him. But before I go any further, there was this big guy that outweighed the other -- the little skinny guy about 60 pounds or so and had four or five inches in height, maybe more. There was another guy in there and he was kind of slender and I believe he was Indian or maybe Chicano or Mexican. So he walked up to this big guy and says, "How about if I take over?" And this big guy looked down and said, "Sure." Well, it turned out this little guy was a light weight boxing champ and he just tattooed that big guy to beat hell. He just tattooed that guy so bad the guy had to plead for mercy and give up. So -- but this guy that I asked for, this skinny guy, turned out that he was the same one that threw me a rope and pulled me out of the river. And also he was the same one who he had a real deep, rich, mellow baritone voice, beautiful singer. He sang at our wedding. So we honeymooned in San Antone and by the time we come back -- it was only three or four days -- his orders had come through and he had already left the camp for his separation center and I never heard from him again. The sad part about it is, I -- I found out that he had marital troubles, that his wife was impregnated by somebody else and I could never locate him. So I don't know whether he's still alive or not. But the fact that I asked for him and the fact that he saved my life, that's stranger than fiction.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned Camp Haus. My dad trained at Camp Haus.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Did he? Yeah?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure did. With the 103rd infantry division.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think there were two divisions that trained there during the war.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. And Gainesville, Texas; right?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I just saw the site -- Camp Haus isn't there anymore but a year and a half ago I saw where it used to be.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: We went down on our 45th anniversary, wedding anniversary. We went down, couldn't even find the house that -- where we used to live. Camp Bowie was gone. Camp Warner was gone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Not a whole lot there.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: But, you know, every time we inquired everybody would say welcome home, welcome home, which was kind of nice. And there's all kinds of incidents.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: When the war ended we were required to wear ODs, Class A uniforms, and we came back to this little town, Campen (ph), Germany, and we just took over apartment houses. Run -- moved the people out and we moved in. And there was a great big quadrangle up in the front where we put up a flag pole and every night we used to have retreat out there and the Germans would always come and watch. You know, we couldn't figure it out. They -- they -- the civilians seemed like they liked military. And so there I am standing in front of the whole company and during retreat and we're at present arms and this little kid comes out of the ranks, little toddler, papa, papa, and he puts both arms around one of my legs, you know, and holding on for dear life. I didn't flinch, nobody flinched in the whole outfit. Nobody laughed. And when it was order arms, you know, his mother was on the sidelines and she was frightened, kind of frantic, and I took him back and she was still very frightened so I said, you know, come with me and I guess -- I guess maybe I didn't do it correctly but she became even more frightened. So I went to my room and got a couple of candy bars and gave it to the little kid and got her pack of cigarettes. We could do that now the war was ended but prior to that, you couldn't fraternize with them, you couldn't talk to any civilians unless it was in the line of duty. Like I said, we used to ask where gravel pits were and -- or, you know, sometimes we would even -- kind of shaded the Geneva -- Geneva convention a little bit. We got some labor out of them. And I won't go any further than that. Best thing about our war, no television, no bleeding heart reporters. They said go out and win it and -- and we did. That's -- the thing that boggles my mind today is that the communication systems, you know, all these guys in Iraq, and they all got their PCs, E-mailing back and forth and cell phones. It boggles my mind.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: But I would like to spend a couple of weeks in a military camp. Not that I could participate in any of their stuff but I sure as heck would make a good observer. I'd like to learn some of what they're doing. As compared to what they're doing now, you know, we were in the Dark Ages. One of my favorite comic strips is BC and we were BC. Before computers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
sp.p: I don't think there's going to be anymore that I can add to that rambling --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay: Do you want me to shut it off?

sp.speaker: Edward Langa
